about.title: San Dimas Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: San Dimas sits at a busy stretch of the San Gabriel Valley where warehouses, distribution centers, and small manufacturing shops operate close to the SR-57 and SR-210 interchange. Workers commuting or driving for work along Arrow Highway or these freeways face the same road hazards reflected in the county's 139 injury collisions and 204 injured people last year. When a workplace injury happens, California generally routes the claim through workers' compensation regardless of fault — but if a subcontractor, equipment manufacturer, property owner, or another driver contributed to the harm, a separate third-party claim may also be possible. Understanding which path applies, and how the two can work together, matters for anyone trying to cover medical bills and lost wages. Our team evaluates both workers' comp claims and any third-party angles worth pursuing for injured San Dimas workers.

items.title: Comp Isn't Always the Whole Picture
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually the exclusive remedy against an employer, but a negligent third party like a subcontractor or equipment maker can still be separately liable. We can help figure out whether that applies to your situation.

items.title: Reporting Deadlines Move Fast
items.desc: California generally requires reporting a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days, so waiting can complicate your options. We can help you understand what's needed before that window closes.

items.title: Retaliation Is Against the Law
items.desc: Employers cannot legally punish you for reporting an injury or filing a claim. If you're worried about your job, we can help you understand your protections.

items.question: I was hurt driving for work near SR-57 in San Dimas — is that workers' comp or a car accident claim?
items.answer: It can be both. Workers' comp may cover medical costs and lost wages regardless of fault, while the driver who hit you could also be liable in a separate third-party claim. We can look at the details and explain how the two claims might work together.

items.question: My employer said I have to use workers' comp and can't sue anyone else — is that true?
items.answer: Workers' comp is usually the exclusive remedy against your employer, but that doesn't automatically block a claim against a third party like a negligent contractor, property owner, or equipment manufacturer. We can review whether someone outside your employer contributed to your injury.

items.question: How long do I have to report my injury and file a claim in California?
items.answer: You generally need to notify your employer within 30 days of a workplace injury to protect your workers' comp rights. If a third party was involved, that separate claim typically carries a two-year deadline. Because these timelines differ, contacting us sooner rather than later can help avoid missed windows.
